The Umayyad Caliphate. From 661 to 750 of the common era, this was the first hereditary Islamic dynasty, centered in Damascus and ruled by Arab aristocracy, which expanded Islamic rule across North Africa and into Spain and Central Asia. Despite its military success and the flowering of early Islamic art and architecture, the Umayyad line was overthrown by the Abbasid Revolution, which promised a more inclusive Islamic state.

The Umayyads were founded by Mu'awiyah I after defeating Ali ibn Abi Talib, shifting from elective to dynastic succession and moving the capital from Medina to Damascus. They conquered North Africa in the 670s and 690s, Spain from 711 to 715, and Central Asia up to the borders of China, making it one of history's largest empires by geographic extent. At the Battle of Tours in 732—halting further Islamic expansion into Western Europe—they were defeated in France. This marked a turning point in medieval history. The Umayyads patronized early Islamic art, calligraphy, and the construction of the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem, establishing enduring aesthetic standards. Yet Arab dominance bred resentment among non-Arab converts, the mawali, and among Shiite communities, creating internal tensions that weakened the dynasty. In 750 they were overthrown by the Abbasid Revolution, which promised a more merit-based caliphate. The last Umayyad surviving prince fled to Spain and established the Umayyad Emirate of Cordoba.

The Rashidun Caliphate came before them with an elective system they replaced with hereditary rule. The Abbasid Caliphate was the revolutionary dynasty that toppled them. They founded Islamic Spain, Al-Andalus, which flourished for three centuries. And the Battle of Tours was the clash that ended Islamic expansion into Europe.
